sections.b: Exodus 20 is the only law the whole people hear directly from God, "from the heavens" (20:22), before they beg Moses to speak for God instead (20:18–21). The Ten Words open with grace, "I am the LORD your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt" (20:2), and then give short commands, most of them beginning "You must not." Exodus calls them "the Ten Words" (34:28) and "the testimony," written by God's finger on two stone tablets (31:18) that are broken and then written again (32:19; 34:1).

The text contains more than ten commands but says there are ten. Jews count "I am the LORD your God" as the first word and join "no other gods" and "no images" as the second. Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, join those two as the first and split the craving command into two: Catholics follow Deuteronomy 5:21 (wife, then goods), while Lutherans follow Exodus 20:17 (house, then wife and the rest). Reformed, Anglican and Orthodox Christians, following Philo, Josephus and Origen, count "no images" separately and keep craving as one. The Samaritans add a command to build an altar on Mount Gerizim. Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5 also differ: "remember" and "keep" the Sabbath, creation and the exodus as its reason, and the order of house and wife.

sections.h: Ten words and all the rest
sections.b: Jewish tradition sees all 613 commandments contained in the ten (Saadia Gaon), and Philo arranged the whole law under them. Jesus quotes the second table to a rich man and sums up the law as love of God and neighbor; Paul says the commands against adultery, murder, theft and craving are summed up in "love your neighbor as yourself." Christian catechisms of every tradition teach the moral life through the ten.

common: The Ten Commandments are the moral core of the Bible's law, binding on all people.
uncommon: Some scholars argue that the original Ten Words were not Exodus 20 but the ritual list in Exodus 34:12–26, which 34:28 calls "the Ten Words."

sections.b: Israel camps before the mountain in the third month after leaving Egypt (Exodus 19:1–2). God offers a covenant: Israel will be his "own private treasure," "a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (19:5–6). The mountain is fenced, the people wash, and on the third day the LORD comes down in fire, cloud and thunder, with a horn blast growing louder (19:16–19). The Ten Words are spoken from there (20), the covenant is sealed with blood at its foot and a meal on its slope (24), and Moses spends forty days in the cloud at its top (24:18).

Christian tradition since the 300s has placed Sinai at Jebel Musa in southern Sinai, under St. Catherine's Monastery. Other proposals include Jebel Serbal, peaks in northern Sinai, Har Karkom in the Negev, and mountains in northwest Arabia, the land of Midian, which some link with Paul's "Mount Sinai in Arabia." None can be proven, and Jewish tradition has often treated the forgotten location as fitting: the Torah, not a place, is what Israel keeps.

Hebrews 12:18–24 contrasts the burning mountain that could not be touched with Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, where believers come to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant. Galatians 4:24–26 uses Sinai for the covenant of slavery and "the Jerusalem above" for freedom. In the Hebrew Bible itself the meaning of Sinai passes to Zion: "from Zion comes teaching" (Isaiah 2:3).

common: Mount Sinai is Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai Peninsula.
uncommon: Some writers place Sinai at Jebel al-Lawz in Saudi Arabia; archaeologists have not accepted the evidence offered for it.

sections.b: A month after leaving Egypt, the hungry people complain, and God promises to "make bread fall like rain from the sky" (Exodus 16:4). Each morning a flaky layer lies on the ground; they ask "What is it?" (man hu) and call it manna (16:15, 31). It tastes like wafers with honey, must be gathered daily, rots if hoarded, and comes double on the sixth day so that the Sabbath can be kept (16:16–30). A jar is kept as a witness (16:32–34), and Israel eats it for forty years (16:35; Joshua 5:12).

Deuteronomy explains the purpose: God fed Israel with manna "to teach you that people do not live by bread alone. People live by everything that comes out of the LORD's mouth" (Deuteronomy 8:3). Jesus quotes this when tempted in the wilderness. Paul quotes the rule that no one had too much or too little (Exodus 16:18) to ask churches to share. Since the 1800s, scientists have compared manna with the honeydew left by insects on tamarisk trees in Sinai.

Exodus 20:22–23:33 is the first law collection after the Ten Words. Exodus 24:7 calls it "the scroll of the covenant." It begins with worship (altars of earth or uncut stone), then gives rulings (mishpatim) on slaves, killing, injuries, oxen, theft and property, and then direct commands: protect the foreigner, the widow and the orphan, lend without interest, judge fairly, rest the land in the seventh year, keep three feasts. It closely resembles Mesopotamian law, especially the laws of Hammurabi, but frames everything as the word of Israel's God and values human life above property.

Exodus 24:12 says God will give Moses "the stone tablets, with the law and the command." The Talmud reads every phrase as a part of revelation, from the Ten Words to the Mishnah and Talmud, all given at Sinai (Berakhot 5a). Rabbinic Judaism counts 613 commandments (Makkot 23b) and reads the law through the oral tradition, so that "eye for eye" means payment (Bava Kamma 84a).

Jesus says he came to fulfill the law, not to abolish it (Matthew 5:17), and Paul calls it "holy" while insisting no one is made right with God by it (Romans 7:12; Galatians 2:16). Lutherans stress the law's power to show sin and drive us to Christ; the Reformed stress its use as a guide for grateful living; Catholics and Orthodox speak of the "new law" of grace written on the heart. Most Christians distinguish the moral law, still binding, from Israel's ceremonial and civil laws.

common: Christians are free from the ceremonial and civil laws of Moses but still bound by the moral law of the Ten Commandments.
uncommon: David Wright argues that the authors of the Covenant Code worked directly from a copy of Hammurabi's laws in the 700s BC.

sections.b: The first rulings of Exodus 21 concern slaves. A Hebrew slave serves six years and goes free in the seventh, unless he chooses to stay and has his ear pierced at the door (21:2–6). A daughter sold as a slave wife keeps rights to food, clothing and marital relations (21:7–11). Kidnapping a person is a capital crime (21:16); a master who kills a slave is punished, and a slave whose eye or tooth is destroyed goes free (21:20–21, 26–27). Yet the same laws call a slave "his money" (21:21), and Leviticus 25:44–46 permits permanent slavery of foreigners.

In the 1800s, American defenders of slavery cited these laws and the New Testament household codes, while abolitionists cited the exodus, Exodus 21:16 against the slave trade, and the image of God in every person. Jewish law narrowed slavery sharply over time. Many readers today say the Bible regulates an institution of its world while planting the principles (God the liberator of slaves, every person in his image, "no longer slave but brother") that finally condemned it.
sections.refs: Exodus 21:16; Genesis 1:27; Deuteronomy 24:7; 1 Timothy 1:10; Philemon 15–16; Galatians 3:28

common: Biblical slavery was mostly temporary debt service and much milder than slavery in the Americas.
uncommon: Some scholars argue that the laws of Exodus 21 were never practiced and are a scribal exercise based on Mesopotamian law.

sections.b: "Life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot" (Exodus 21:23–25) appears in a ruling about an injured pregnant woman and is repeated in Leviticus 24:19–20 and Deuteronomy 19:21. Hammurabi's laws have similar rules but apply them only between equals and replace them with fines for commoners and slaves. In Exodus the principle applies to all free people alike, and it is right away followed by a slave's freedom for a lost eye or tooth (21:26–27). The point is proportion: no more than the harm done, as against Lamech's seventy-sevenfold revenge (Genesis 4:23–24).

The rabbis taught that the law means monetary compensation, arguing that a literal eye could never equal another and noting that only for murder does the Torah forbid a ransom (Numbers 35:31; Bava Kamma 83b–84a; Mekhilta). Josephus mentions that a victim could accept payment. Jesus quotes the principle and tells his followers not to resist an evildoer but to turn the other cheek (Matthew 5:38–42); Christians debate whether this governs personal revenge only or also courts and war.

common: "An eye for an eye" was a cruel law that Jesus replaced with mercy.
uncommon: Some scholars think talion was meant literally in Israel's earliest courts and was softened to payment only later.

sections.b: After the exodus, Jethro brings Zipporah and her sons to Moses at the mountain of God (Exodus 18:1–6). He rejoices at what the LORD has done, declares "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods," offers sacrifices, and eats a meal with Aaron and the elders "before God" (18:9–12). Seeing Moses judge alone from morning to evening, he advises him to appoint capable, God-fearing, honest men over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens (18:13–26). Deuteronomy 1:9–18 tells the appointment without mentioning him.

The rabbis debated whether Jethro came before or after the Torah was given and called him a righteous convert, giving his name to the Torah portion that contains the Ten Commandments. Modern scholars ask whether Jethro's Midianite or Kenite people taught Israel to worship the LORD, pointing to the Kenites' later closeness to Israel; others answer that Jethro here confesses the LORD as something newly learned.

Joshua first appears leading Israel against Amalek while Moses holds up his hands (Exodus 17:8–13). He is Moses' "helper" who goes partway up Sinai (24:13), mistakes the noise of the golden calf for war (32:17), and stays in the tent of meeting when Moses leaves (33:11). Moses renames him from Hoshea to Joshua, "the LORD saves" (Numbers 13:16), and he and Caleb alone among the spies trust God's promise.
sections.refs: Exodus 17:8–14; Exodus 24:13; Exodus 32:17; Exodus 33:11; Numbers 11:28; Numbers 13:16; Numbers 14:6–9

sections.b: In Greek, Joshua and Jesus are the same name, Iēsous, and Hebrews 4:8 uses it of Joshua. Early Christian writers made much of this: Barnabas and Justin Martyr saw Joshua's victory over Amalek, won while Moses' arms were stretched out, as a picture of Jesus and the cross. The rabbis made Joshua the first link in the chain of tradition: "Moses received the Torah at Sinai and handed it to Joshua" (Avot 1:1).

Amalek attacks Israel at Rephidim, the first battle after the sea (Exodus 17:8). Joshua fights while Moses stands on a hill with the staff; Israel wins while his hands are raised, held up by Aaron and Hur. God tells Moses to write a record: "I will wipe out, yes, wipe out the memory of Amalek from beneath the sky," and Moses names the altar "The LORD Is My Flag," saying, "The LORD will war with Amalek, one generation after another" (17:14–16). Deuteronomy 25:17–19 adds that Amalek struck the weary stragglers.

The Mishnah's teaching that the Assyrian king Sennacherib mixed up the nations (Yadayim 4:4) was used to hold that ancient peoples like Amalek can no longer be identified. Many Jewish teachers read Amalek as the evil within, the doubt that asks "Is the LORD here with us, or isn't he?" (Exodus 17:7). Others warn that naming modern enemies "Amalek" has been used to justify violence.

sections.h: Sabbath in the wilderness and at Sinai
sections.b: The Sabbath is first commanded to Israel with the manna: a double portion on the sixth day, nothing on the seventh (Exodus 16:22–30). At Sinai it becomes the fourth (Jewish, Reformed) or third (Catholic, Lutheran) commandment, with creation as its reason: "in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth" (20:8–11). Exodus 23:12 gives a humane reason: so that the ox, the donkey, the slave and the foreigner may catch their breath. The seventh-year rest for the land feeds the poor and the wild animals (23:10–11).

At Sinai God offers Israel a covenant based on what he has already done: "I lifted you up on the wings of eagles and brought you to me" (Exodus 19:4). Its terms are the Ten Words and the Covenant Code (20–23). In chapter 24 Moses reads the scroll of the covenant, the people promise "we will do, and we will listen," and Moses splashes blood on the altar and the people: "Here is the blood of the covenant" (24:7–8). Scholars compare this pattern with ancient treaties between kings and their subjects. Jesus' words at the Last Supper echo 24:8.
sections.refs: Exodus 19:3–8; Exodus 24:3–11; Deuteronomy 5:2–3; Jeremiah 31:31–34; Mark 14:24; Hebrews 9:18–22

sections.h: The Feast of Harvest and the giving of the Torah
sections.b: Exodus 23:16 calls it "the Feast of Harvest, for the first crops of your work." It is one of three times a year when all males must appear before the LORD (23:14–17). Because Israel reached Sinai in the third month (19:1), the rabbis dated the giving of the Torah to the sixth of Sivan, the day of Shavuot (Shabbat 86b), and the Book of Jubilees already makes the feast a renewal of the covenant. Jews read Exodus 19–20 in synagogue on Shavuot.

sections.h: "You know the life of a foreigner"
sections.b: The Covenant Code twice forbids oppressing the foreigner, the ger, for the same reason: "you were foreigners living in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 22:21; 23:9). The second adds, "You know the life of a foreigner from the inside," literally "the soul of the foreigner." The foreigner also shares the Sabbath rest (20:10; 23:12). The rabbis counted many such warnings in the Torah and read ger as the convert (Bava Metzia 59b).

"Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly. If you do treat him harshly, and he cries out to me, be sure I will hear his cry" (Exodus 22:22–23). God threatens that the oppressor's own wife will become a widow and his children orphans (22:24), measure for measure. The same chapter forbids charging interest to the poor and keeping a poor man's cloak overnight, "for I am gracious" (22:25–27).

Exodus 24:9–11 is the Bible's boldest vision of God: Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy elders "saw the God of Israel," with a floor like blue lapis under his feet, and he did not harm them; "they looked upon God, and they ate and drank." The Greek translation softened it to "the place where the God of Israel stood," and Targum Onqelos to "the glory of the God of Israel." Only a few chapters later God says "no human being can see me and stay alive" (33:20). The Talmud took the meal as a picture of the world to come, where the righteous feast on the radiance of God's presence (Berakhot 17a).

When Jesus gives the cup at the Last Supper, his words, "This is my blood of the covenant" (Mark 14:24; Matthew 26:28), repeat what Moses said when he threw the sacrificial blood on the people at Sinai: "Here is the blood of the covenant" (Exodus 24:8). Luke and Paul add "new covenant," from Jeremiah 31:31. The covenant meal on the mountain (Exodus 24:11) has also been read as a forerunner of the Lord's table and the wedding supper of the Lamb.
sections.refs: Exodus 24:8–11; Mark 14:24; Matthew 26:28; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; Hebrews 9:18–22; Revelation 19:9

sections.b: In Exodus 16–24 Moses feeds the people, strikes water from the rock, holds up his hands over the battle with Amalek, accepts Jethro's advice to share the work of judging, and becomes the go-between at Sinai: the people ask him to speak for God (20:19), and he alone enters "the deep darkness where God was" (20:21). He writes down the words of the LORD, seals the covenant with blood, and goes up into the cloud for forty days (24:4–8, 18). Deuteronomy 18:15–18 promises "a prophet like me," which Acts applies to Jesus.
sections.refs: Exodus 17:8–13; Exodus 18:13–26; Exodus 20:18–21; Exodus 24:1–18; Deuteronomy 18:15–18; Acts 3:22–23

sections.b: At the foot of Sinai Moses builds an altar and sets up "twelve standing stones for the twelve tribes of Israel" (Exodus 24:4). In the same law collection, Israel must smash the standing stones of Canaan's gods (23:24). The difference lies in what the stone stands for: a witness to the covenant with the LORD, as with Joshua's stone at Shechem (Joshua 24:26–27), or the presence of another god.

sections.h: The messenger who bears God's name
sections.b: "Here, I am sending an angel in front of you to keep you safe on the way" (Exodus 23:20). Israel must listen to his voice, for "my name is in him," and he will not forgive their rebellion (23:21). Some rabbis identified this angel with Metatron (Sanhedrin 38b); many church fathers saw the pre-incarnate Son. Mark 1:2 joins the words of 23:20 with Malachi 3:1 for John the Baptist.

God's first words at Sinai recall the exodus: "I lifted you up on the wings of eagles and brought you to me" (Exodus 19:4). Deuteronomy 32:11 develops the picture of an eagle stirring its nest and catching its young on its wings, and Isaiah 40:31 promises that those who wait for the LORD will rise up on wings like eagles. Rashi said the eagle carries its young on its back, so that any arrow must pass through the eagle first.
